lessons.title: Classification of living organisms
lessons.summary: Learn how Linnaeus sorted life into seven ranks, how binomial names work, why Woese introduced three domains, and how to read an evolutionary tree.
objectives: I can list the Linnaean ranks in order from kingdom to species and explain what they are based on.
I can write a binomial name correctly and explain what it tells us about relationships.
I can describe how microscopes, biochemistry and Carl Woese's work led to the three-domain system.
I can interpret an evolutionary tree and explain where the evidence for it comes from.

activities.title: Sorting life into groups
activities.content:
## Why do we classify?

Biologists have named nearly two million species, and there are many more still to find. To make sense of this variety we **classify** organisms: we sort them into groups based on the features they share.

The system used today was set up in the 1700s by the Swedish scientist **Carl Linnaeus**. He grouped organisms by their **structure and characteristics** - things he could observe, such as whether an animal had a backbone, fur or feathers, or how many petals a flower had.

## The seven ranks

Linnaeus arranged living things into groups nested inside groups:

| Rank | Example (humans) |
|---|---|
| Kingdom | Animalia |
| Phylum | Chordata |
| Class | Mammalia |
| Order | Primates |
| Family | Hominidae |
| Genus | *Homo* |
| Species | *sapiens* |

A handy way to remember the order: **K**ing **P**rawn **C**urry **O**r **F**ish **G**ets **S**oggy.

As you move down the table the groups get **smaller** and the organisms in them share **more features**. A kingdom holds millions of species; a species holds only organisms that can breed together to produce **fertile offspring**.

**Exam tip:** you may be asked to name the ranks in order, or to say which rank is the largest (kingdom) or the smallest (species).

activities.title: Worked example: where does a cat fit?
activities.content:
**Task:** classify the domestic cat and compare it with a lion and a dog.

| Rank | Domestic cat | Lion | Dog |
|---|---|---|---|
| Kingdom | Animalia | Animalia | Animalia |
| Phylum | Chordata | Chordata | Chordata |
| Class | Mammalia | Mammalia | Mammalia |
| Order | Carnivora | Carnivora | Carnivora |
| Family | Felidae | Felidae | Canidae |
| Genus | *Felis* | *Panthera* | *Canis* |
| Species | *catus* | *leo* | *familiaris* |

**Reasoning**

1. All three are animals with backbones, fur and milk-producing glands, so they share kingdom, phylum and class.
2. All three eat meat and have specialised teeth, so they share the order Carnivora.
3. The cat and lion are both members of the cat family, Felidae - retractable claws and a similar skull shape. The dog is in a different family.
4. The cat and lion differ at genus level, so they are separate genera as well as separate species.

**Conclusion:** the domestic cat is more closely related to the lion (shared down to family) than to the dog (shared only down to order). The lower the shared rank, the closer the relationship.

question.text: Put these Linnaean ranks in order, starting with the **largest** group. (Two ranks have been left out.)
question.hint: Think of the mnemonic: King Prawn Curry Or Fish Gets Soggy.
question.explanation: The full order is kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species. Removing phylum and order leaves: kingdom, class, family, genus, species.

activities.title: Binomial names
activities.content:
## Two-part names

Common names cause confusion. In Britain a *robin* is a small brown bird with a red breast; in North America the bird called a robin is a much larger thrush. Scientists in different countries need a name that means the same thing everywhere.

Linnaeus solved this with the **binomial system**. Every species gets a two-part Latin name:

- the **genus** comes first and starts with a **capital** letter
- the **species** comes second and is all **lower case**
- the whole name is written in *italics* in print, or **underlined** when handwritten

So humans are *Homo sapiens*, the lion is *Panthera leo* and the tiger is *Panthera tigris*. Once the full name has been used, it can be shortened to *H. sapiens*.

## What the name tells you

Organisms in the same genus are **closely related**. The lion and tiger share the genus *Panthera*, so they are more closely related to each other than either is to the domestic cat, *Felis catus*.

## Why it matters

- one agreed name for each species, used by scientists worldwide
- avoids mix-ups caused by local names and languages
- shows relationships at a glance

**Exam tip:** if you are asked to write a binomial name, check the capital letter, the lower-case species and the order.

activities.title: Worked example: spot the mistake
activities.content:
A student writes the name of our own species four ways. Which is correct?

| Written by student | Correct? | Problem |
|---|---|---|
| homo sapiens | No | genus needs a capital H |
| Homo Sapiens | No | species must be lower case |
| *Homo sapiens* | Yes | capital genus, lower-case species, italics |
| Sapiens homo | No | genus must come first |

**Using the names to find relationships**

The leopard is *Panthera pardus* and the jaguar is *Panthera onca*. Both share the genus *Panthera*, so they are closely related - more closely than either is to the cheetah, *Acinonyx jubatus*, which is in a different genus.

**But are they the same species?** No. Different second names mean different species. Even though closely related big cats can occasionally breed in captivity, their offspring are usually infertile, so they fail the test for being one species (producing *fertile* offspring).

**Exam tip:** if you are asked what a binomial name tells you, mention **both** parts: the genus shows the group of closely related species, and the species name identifies one particular species within it.

question.text: The grey wolf belongs to the genus *Canis* and the species *lupus*. Which option shows its binomial name written correctly?
question.hint: Genus first with a capital letter; species second in lower case.
question.explanation: *Canis lupus* is correct: the genus *Canis* comes first with a capital C, and the species *lupus* is all lower case. The other options either swap the order or use the wrong capitals.

options.feedback: The genus must start with a capital letter.
The species name is always lower case.
The genus comes first, then the species.

activities.title: New evidence, new groups
activities.content:
## Classification keeps improving

Linnaeus could only use what he saw with the naked eye. Two big developments let scientists look deeper:

1. **Better microscopes** revealed the internal structure of cells. Biologists could see that some cells have a nucleus (eukaryotes) and some do not (prokaryotes), and could study tiny organisms such as bacteria in detail.
2. **Biochemistry** - understanding the chemical processes inside organisms - let scientists compare molecules such as proteins, DNA and RNA rather than just body shape.

## Woese's three domains

In 1977 the American microbiologist **Carl Woese** used **chemical analysis** (comparing the sequence of a type of RNA found in ribosomes) to propose a new top level above kingdom: the **domain**. There are three:

| Domain | What it contains |
|---|---|
| **Archaea** | primitive bacteria, often living in extreme environments such as hot springs |
| **Bacteria** | true bacteria, for example *E. coli* |
| **Eukaryota** | protists, fungi, plants and animals - all have cells with a nucleus |

Woese's evidence showed that Archaea and Bacteria, although they look similar, are chemically very different and separated a very long time ago. The three-domain system is now widely accepted, with the kingdoms sitting underneath the domains.

**Exam tip:** be ready to name all three domains and to say that the evidence came from **chemical analysis**.

activities.title: Worked example: why three domains?
activities.content:
Under a light microscope, Archaea and Bacteria look almost identical: both are tiny single cells with no nucleus. So why did Woese put them in different domains?

**Step 1 - the evidence.** Woese compared the sequence of **ribosomal RNA**, a molecule every living cell uses to build proteins. Because it changes very slowly over time, the number of differences between two organisms shows how long ago they separated.

**Step 2 - the result.** The RNA of Archaea was as different from Bacteria as it was from plants and animals. In some ways Archaea were chemically closer to eukaryotes.

**Step 3 - the conclusion.** Life should be split into three deep groups, not two:

```
        common ancestor of all life
             /        |        \
       Bacteria    Archaea    Eukaryota
                               /  |   |   \
                        protists fungi plants animals
```

**Other differences found later**

| Feature | Bacteria | Archaea |
|---|---|---|
| Cell wall chemistry | contains peptidoglycan | no peptidoglycan |
| Typical habitat | almost everywhere | often extreme: hot, salty or acidic |

This is a good example of how **new evidence** (chemical analysis) led scientists to **change an accepted model** - something examiners like you to recognise.

question.text: Match each domain in Woese's system to its description.
question.hint: Only one domain has cells with a nucleus.
question.explanation: Archaea are primitive bacteria often found in extreme places; Bacteria are the true bacteria; Eukaryota includes every organism whose cells have a nucleus - protists, fungi, plants and animals.

pairs.right: Primitive bacteria, often living in extreme environments such as hot springs
True bacteria such as E. coli
Organisms whose cells have a nucleus: protists, fungi, plants and animals

activities.title: Evolutionary trees
activities.content:
## Reading an evolutionary tree

An **evolutionary tree** is a diagram that shows how closely related different organisms are and how they are thought to have evolved from **common ancestors**.

- The **tips** of the branches are the organisms (living or extinct).
- Each **branch point** is a common ancestor that split into two groups.
- The **more recent** the branch point two organisms share, the **more closely related** they are.
- Time usually runs from the bottom (oldest) to the top (present day), or from left to right.

## Where the evidence comes from

| Organisms | Evidence used |
|---|---|
| Living | **classification data** - structure and, increasingly, DNA and protein comparisons |
| Extinct | the **fossil record** - fossils show what ancestors looked like and when they lived |

If two species share a large proportion of their DNA, they split from a common ancestor recently. If fossils show a feature appearing at a certain time, the branch carrying that feature must begin after that date.

**Exam tip:** in tree questions, always trace back from each organism until the lines meet. The pair whose lines meet **closest to the tips** is the most closely related. The organism that joins the others at the **oldest** branch point is the least related.

activities.title: Worked example: reading a tree
activities.content:
Here is a simplified evolutionary tree for four animals. Time runs upwards, so the top is the present day.

```
present   Toad    Frog    Newt    Lizard
            \      /       |        |
             \    /        |        |
              (A)          |        |
                \          |        |
                 \         |        |
                  (B)------+        |
                    \               |
                     \              |
                      (C)-----------+
 past
```

**Q: Which two animals are most closely related?**
The toad and the frog - their lines meet at A, the most recent branch point.

**Q: Which branch point is the common ancestor of the frog and the newt?**
Trace back from each until the lines meet: B.

**Q: Which animal is least closely related to the others?**
The lizard - it joins at C, the oldest branch point.

**Q: Fossils of ancestor B are 250 million years old. What can you say about A?**
A is above B on the tree, so the toad and frog separated **more recently** than 250 million years ago.

**Q: Where did the data for this tree come from?**
For the living species, classification data such as skeletal structure and DNA comparisons; for the ancestors A, B and C, fossils.

question.text: Complete the sentences about evolutionary trees.

metadata.blanksText: In an evolutionary tree, each branch point represents a common ___. Trees for living organisms are built from classification data, including comparisons of ___ sequences, whereas trees for extinct organisms rely on the ___ record.

question.hint: The second blank is the molecule that carries genetic information; the third is what we dig out of rocks.
question.explanation: Branch points are common ancestors. For living organisms scientists compare DNA (and other molecules); for extinct organisms the only evidence is the fossil record.

question.text:
The common kingfisher is *Alcedo atthis*. The azure kingfisher is *Alcedo azurea*.

A student says: "The names show that the two birds belong to the same species."

(a) Explain why the student is wrong, and state what the names **do** tell you about the two birds. **(2 marks)**

(b) Explain why scientists use binomial names instead of common names. **(1 mark)**

(c) Describe how Carl Woese used new evidence to change the way organisms are classified. **(2 marks)**
question.hint: Look at which part of the name is shared and which part is different. For (c), think about what kind of evidence Woese used and what new top-level groups he proposed.
question.explanation: (a) The second word is different, so they are different species; the shared first word means they are in the same genus and are therefore closely related. (b) Common names vary between countries and languages, so one agreed Latin name lets scientists worldwide be sure they mean the same organism. (c) Woese used chemical analysis (comparing RNA sequences) and proposed three domains - Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota - above the level of kingdom.

markScheme.criterion: Different species names mean they are different species
Same genus (Alcedo) so they are closely related
Binomial names are the same worldwide / avoid confusion caused by local names
Woese used chemical analysis / RNA comparisons
Proposed the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukaryota)

activities.title: Key points
activities.content:
- **Linnaeus** classified organisms by structure and characteristics into **kingdom, phylum, class, order, family, genus, species** (groups get smaller and more similar as you go down).
- **Binomial names**: *Genus species* - capital genus, lower-case species, italics or underlined. Same genus = closely related; a universal name avoids confusion.
- **Microscopes** (cell structure) and **biochemistry** (DNA, RNA, proteins) improved classification.
- **Carl Woese** used chemical analysis to propose the **three domains**: Archaea, Bacteria, Eukaryota.
- **Evolutionary trees** show common ancestors; built from classification data for living organisms and **fossils** for extinct ones. The more recent the shared branch point, the closer the relationship.

practiceQuestions.text: True or false: in a binomial name, the genus is written second.
practiceQuestions.hint: Think about *Homo sapiens* - which word is the genus?
practiceQuestions.explanation: False. The genus comes first (with a capital letter) and the species second, as in *Homo sapiens*.

practiceQuestions.text: Which Linnaean rank contains the **fewest** organisms, all sharing the most features?
practiceQuestions.hint: It is the last rank in the list and the one used in binomial names.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Species is the smallest rank. All the members of a species can breed together to produce fertile offspring.

practiceQuestions.text: Select all that apply. Which of the following are **domains** in the three-domain system?
practiceQuestions.hint: Domains sit above kingdoms, so kingdom names are not domains.
practiceQuestions.explanation: The three domains are Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota. Fungi and Animalia are kingdoms inside the domain Eukaryota.

options.feedback: Fungi is a kingdom within Eukaryota.
Animalia is a kingdom within Eukaryota.

practiceQuestions.text: Scientists compare a 1500-base section of the same gene in two species. They find that 45 bases are different. Calculate the percentage of bases that differ.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 45 ÷ 1500 = 0.03, and 0.03 × 100 = 3 %. A small percentage difference suggests the two species separated fairly recently.

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about the Linnaean system.

metadata.blanksText: Linnaeus classified organisms according to their ___ and characteristics. The seven ranks run from ___ (the largest group) down to ___ (the smallest group).

practiceQuestions.hint: The first blank is about the body features he could observe.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Linnaeus used structure and characteristics. The ranks go from kingdom at the top to species at the bottom.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each scientist or development to its contribution to classification.
practiceQuestions.hint: One scientist worked in the 1700s with only his eyes; the other worked in the 1970s with molecules.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Linnaeus created the ranks and binomial naming from observable features. Better microscopes revealed cell structure. Biochemistry allowed molecules to be compared. Woese used RNA analysis to propose the three domains.

pairs.right: Devised the seven-rank system and binomial naming based on observable features
Proposed the three domains using chemical (RNA) analysis
Revealed cell structure, such as whether a nucleus is present
Allowed DNA, RNA and proteins to be compared between organisms

practiceQuestions.text: These are the groups that humans belong to at different ranks. Put them in order from the **largest** group to the **smallest**. (Species has been left out.)
practiceQuestions.hint: Kingdom comes first. Genus is the last one here.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Kingdom Animalia, phylum Chordata, class Mammalia, order Primates, family Hominidae, genus *Homo* (then species *sapiens*).

practiceQuestions.text: The brown bear is *Ursus arctos* and the polar bear is *Ursus maritimus*. What do the names tell you about how the two bears are related, and why are they still classed as separate species?
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the first words, then the second words.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Both are in the genus *Ursus*, so they are closely related and share a recent common ancestor. Their species names are different, so they are separate species - in the wild they do not normally interbreed to produce fertile offspring.

markScheme.criterion: Different species names / cannot normally produce fertile offspring together

practiceQuestions.text:
The evolutionary tree shows four small mammals. Time runs upwards; the top is the present day.

```
present  Hedgehog   Mole    Shrew    Bat
             \       /        |       |
              \     /         |       |
               (P)            |       |
                 \            |       |
                  (Q)---------+       |
                    \                 |
                     (R)--------------+
 past
```

(a) Which two animals are the most closely related? **(1 mark)**

(b) Which animal is the least closely related to the other three? **(1 mark)**

(c) A fossil of ancestor Q is dated at 60 million years old. What does this tell you about when the hedgehog and the mole separated from each other? **(1 mark)**

(d) Suggest one type of evidence scientists could use to build the tree for the **living** species. **(1 mark)**
practiceQuestions.hint: Trace back from each animal until the lines meet. The most recent meeting point means the closest relationship.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) Hedgehog and mole - they share the most recent branch point, P. (b) The bat, which joins the others at R, the oldest branch point. (c) P is more recent than Q, so the hedgehog and mole separated less than 60 million years ago. (d) DNA (or protein) comparisons, or other classification data such as skeletal structure.

markScheme.criterion: They separated more recently than / less than 60 million years ago
DNA / protein / RNA comparison or other classification data

practiceQuestions.text: Explain how developments in microscopes and in biochemistry have improved the classification of organisms.
practiceQuestions.hint: What could each development show that Linnaeus could not see? What was the result for how organisms are grouped?
practiceQuestions.explanation: Better microscopes revealed the internal structure of cells, such as whether a nucleus is present, so prokaryotes and eukaryotes could be separated. Biochemistry allowed molecules such as DNA, RNA and proteins to be compared, showing how closely organisms are related. Together this evidence led to new groupings, such as Woese's three domains, that reflect evolutionary relationships more accurately.

markScheme.criterion: Microscopes revealed cell structure / internal features (e.g. presence of a nucleus)
Biochemistry allowed comparison of molecules such as DNA, RNA or proteins
Led to new / more accurate groupings, e.g. the three domains

practiceQuestions.text: On a scale drawing of an evolutionary tree, 1 cm represents 5 million years. The branch point where two species separated is drawn 3.6 cm below the present-day line. How many million years ago did the two species separate?
practiceQuestions.hint: Multiply the distance by the number of million years each centimetre represents.
practiceQuestions.explanation: 3.6 cm × 5 million years per cm = 18 million years ago.

practiceQuestions.text: Put these Linnaean ranks in order, starting with the **smallest** group. (Two ranks have been left out.)
practiceQuestions.hint: Species is the smallest group. Then work back up the list: King Prawn Curry Or Fish Gets Soggy, in reverse.
practiceQuestions.explanation: From smallest to largest the full order is species, genus, family, order, class, phylum, kingdom. Leaving out class and kingdom gives: species, genus, family, order, phylum.

practiceQuestions.text: The house sparrow belongs to the genus *Passer* and the species *domesticus*. Which option shows its binomial name written correctly?
practiceQuestions.hint: The genus comes first and starts with a capital letter; the species comes second, all in lower case.
practiceQuestions.explanation: *Passer domesticus* is correct: genus first with a capital P, species second in lower case. The other options swap the order or use the wrong capital letters.

options.feedback: The genus name must begin with a capital letter.
The species name is always written in lower case.
The genus is written first, then the species.

practiceQuestions.text: Match each organism to the domain it belongs to in Woese's three-domain system.
practiceQuestions.hint: Any organism whose cells contain a nucleus is a eukaryote; the primitive bacteria found in extreme places are archaea.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Methane-producing microorganisms from a hot spring are archaea, the primitive bacteria that often live in extreme conditions. Salmonella is a true bacterium. A mushroom is a fungus, and fungal cells have a nucleus, so it belongs to the Eukaryota.

pairs.left: A methane-producing microorganism living in a hot spring
Salmonella, a cause of food poisoning
A mushroom, whose cells contain a nucleus

practiceQuestions.text: Complete the sentences about what an evolutionary tree shows.

metadata.blanksText: An evolutionary tree is a diagram that shows how closely different species are ___. The more recently two species shared a common ancestor, the more ___ their DNA base sequences are. Species whose branches split off from each other a very long time ago are only ___ related.

practiceQuestions.hint: The first and third blanks are about how close the relationship is; the second describes DNA that has few differences.
practiceQuestions.explanation: Evolutionary trees show how closely species are related. Species that split from a common ancestor recently have had little time to build up differences, so their DNA is very similar. Species that split long ago are only distantly related.

practiceQuestions.text:
The red fox is *Vulpes vulpes*. The Arctic fox is *Vulpes lagopus*.

A student says: "Both names start with *Vulpes*, so the two foxes must be the same species."

(a) Explain why the student is wrong, and state what the names **do** tell you about the two foxes. **(2 marks)**

(b) Explain why scientists working in different countries prefer to use binomial names rather than common names. **(1 mark)**

(c) Describe how Carl Woese's classification system differs from the Linnaean system, and state what evidence he used to develop it. **(2 marks)**
practiceQuestions.hint: Compare the two parts of each name separately. For (c), think about the new top level of classification Woese added and the kind of chemical evidence he used.
practiceQuestions.explanation: (a) The second word of the name is different, so they are different species; the shared first word shows they are in the same genus and so are closely related. (b) Common names change from one country and language to another, so a single agreed Latin name means scientists everywhere know they are discussing the same organism. (c) Woese added a new level above kingdom, dividing life into three domains (Archaea, Bacteria and Eukaryota), based on chemical analysis comparing the RNA of different organisms.

markScheme.criterion: Different species names mean they are different species
Same genus (Vulpes) so they are closely related
Binomial names are the same worldwide / avoid confusion caused by local names
Woese proposed the three-domain system (Archaea, Bacteria, Eukaryota) above kingdom
Based on chemical analysis / comparing RNA
